title: The letter of victory
hook: from the wilderness the Guru writes to the emperor Aurangzeb in Persian, rebuking broken oaths
tomorrow: Nanded, 1708: the Guru is the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chali Mukte, the forty who left and came back, and the paper the Guru tore up. Your line was you can always come back.
screen: `CHALI MUKTE — YOU CAN ALWAYS COME BACK.`

segments.voice: There's the letter written in fury, and the letter that actually gets sent: shorter, and harder to argue with. Here is a man who has lost almost everything. His city is gone. His mother is gone. All four of his sons are gone, two in battle and two behind a wall. In a small village in the dry country of Punjab, with a handful of followers, he picks up a pen and writes to the emperor himself, Aurangzeb. He calls it a letter of victory.
screen: `THE LETTER THAT GETS SENT.` → `EVERYTHING LOST.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Zafarnama. Zafar is victory; nama, a letter or a book. Guru Gobind Singh wrote it in Persian, the language of the Mughal court, in verse: a little over a hundred couplets. Tradition says two Sikhs, Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh, carried it all the way south to the emperor's camp in the Deccan. It opens the way a letter to a king would, with praise, but the praise is for God, not the king. Then it turns to the emperor, and it doesn't flatter. At Anandpur, the letter says, your commanders swore oaths, on the Qur'an itself, that the Guru and his people could leave in safety. The moment they left, they were attacked. The Guru writes as someone who takes an oath seriously, and holds the emperor to his own faith's promise. One couplet Sikhs often quote says, in paraphrase, that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Sikhs read it carefully: not a love of fighting, but a last resort, after every other door is shut. So why victory? The Guru had no army to speak of and no home. The victory is in the telling: truth, said plainly to the face of power, by a man with nothing left to lose. Tradition says the emperor was shaken by it, and that he died not long after, in 1707. Historians aren't sure he ever read it. Sikhs keep it in the Dasam Granth, the collection of writings linked to the tenth Guru, and still read it aloud.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA — THE LETTER OF VICTORY.` · `IN PERSIAN, TO THE EMPEROR.` · `YOU SWORE ON THE QUR'AN, AND BROKE IT.` · `THE SWORD ONLY WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.` · then, large: `VICTORY IS THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Think of something true you haven't said, to someone who let you down, to someone you let down, or just to yourself. Find one sentence for it: not the angry draft, the short one, clear, honest and without cruelty. Write it down if you have paper, or say it once silently; you don't have to send it.
Zafarnama. The letter of victory, written in Persian by Guru Gobind Singh to the emperor Aurangzeb, holding him to his broken oaths.
Your line: victory is the truth. A short letter, and an emperor held to his word. Day ninety-two, done.

screen: `DAY 92 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NANDED, 1708: THE GURU IS THE GRANTH.`

howItsDone: The Zafarnama is kept in the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs read and recite it, often in the original Persian, especially when remembering the events of 1704 to 1706.

notes: Number of couplets: commonly given as 111 (some count differently); the script says 'a little over a hundred'. Confirm.
Place and date of composition: tradition places it at Dina (Kangar), around 1705-06; the script says only 'a small village in the dry country'. Confirm the order relative to Khidrana (day 91).
The 'last resort' couplet is paraphrased, not quoted; no public-domain translation was used. Confirm the paraphrase.
'All four of his sons are gone' before the letter: consistent with days 89-90; confirm.
Oaths sworn on the Qur'an (and, in some accounts, by the hill rajas on the cow): the script mentions only the Qur'an. Confirm that framing is fair and handled respectfully.
Whether Aurangzeb read the letter is historically uncertain; stated so.
